posts.title: Abu Dhabi rediscovered through new app
posts.markdown: Photo via deriveapp.com There is always an excuse – it’s too hot, I have work to do, and the classic, there is nowhere to go. These are lines that we sling around like catchphrases as we sit, safe and comfortable, in the confines of Sama Tower, unwilling to venture past the glossy metal gates of our lobby and into the heat and smog of the city. We make up excuses for why we don’t leave Sama Tower as the city lurks in our bedroom windows. But where does this unwillingness to explore stem from? In a university so familiar with the itch of wanderlust, it is strange that a common complaint is that we rarely leave our dormitories. The absence of a walking culture in Abu Dhabi is a major issue among the student body. In professor Pascal Menoret’s class, Politics and the City, students met with app developers Eduardo Cachuco and Babak Fakhamzadeh to create a virtual walking guide for the city during a weekend workshop. The guide, which comes as a downloadable app for smartphones, is called the Dérive app. The name stems from the Situationist movement in France during the 1950s and 1960s, when people fought to combat commercialism and commodification by encouraging more thoughtful relations to objects and surroundings. The idea of Dérive is not to provide set destinations. It is something different from the little virtual red pushpins that we rely on when we we use Google Maps to trace our path from one point to another. In fact, the app is the enemy of the little red pushpin – its aim is not to provide routes, but rather to offer tasks or instigators that help refresh one’s perception in the city. These tasks come in cards that you can shuffle with just a tap of an iPhone screen, and they range from requests like turn at the next red light, to follow an alley to its end to something as simple as find silence. The Dérive app, which already has versions designed for cities such as New York, consists of a general set of cards as well as cards that are specifically geared towards one city. It may just be what NYUAD students need to brave the sometimes confusing layout of Abu Dhabi. The unique features of Abu Dhabi’s urban landscape presented a challenge for members of the creative workshop. The abundance of superblocks and the lanes of traffic that double as pedestrian obstacle courses are two factors that students cite as major struggles when getting to know the city. “The city is a city that is ostensibly built for cars,” says Charlotte Wang, a participant in the workshop and a junior at NYUAD. “Most of its major pathways are built for cars, so as a walker you’re limited.” The lack of pedestrian-friendly paths leads to students developing quick, easy routes to where they need to go, routes that they rarely stray from. “The problem is, we tend to be constrained by the grid and go from Point A to Point B by using big avenues and boring sidewalks," Menoret said. "If we learned to get lost, it would actually make the city more interesting, more livable, more walk-able. [Dérive is] a very cool app that helps you randomize your experience of the city.” On the first day of the workshop, co-organized with professor Dale Hudson, the students of Menoret’s class went out into the city with the app’s set of general tasks and took notes on their different experiences. The following day, they used these observations to create a special set for Abu Dhabi. The cards, which are also translated into Arabic, have illustrations that were designed by students and faculty of Abu Dhabi. “What the Dérive app forces you to notice is these everyday things that we overlook,” Wang said. “For example, we had a couple of directives like follow a pedestrian. I’d never noticed how much people walk all over the place. It’s almost chaotic because there’s no set pattern that people are following. I hadn’t noticed that until we were asked to follow someone within a superblock.” Jennifer Acker, a creative writing professor at NYUAD who is interested in the organization of cities, also attended the workshop. “I enjoyed thinking about how these cards were or were not pushing me in directions other than what I would have come up with on my own,” Acker said. “I wouldn’t say that the Dérive app changed my impression of the city, but it did show me a way to create something playful and fun and to pay attention to new things.” The app user can upload pictures of their journey to the Dérive website, as well as offer feedback for future cards. The Dérive combines social media with urban exploration in order to abolish the set, comfortable paths in a city that people often rely on – such as the short walks to DTC and Al Safa – and create something new. Freshman Nushkia Chamba, who also participated in the Dérive tour, said that the app prompted her to be creative and imaginative in her walking. “There was no clearly defined path, and we could actually walk between cars, go around them, or go behind a building,” says Chamba. “We had to create our own path.” Zoe Hu is deputy news editor. Email her at thegazelle.org@gmail.com.

posts.title: On the UAE and Public Art
posts.markdown:
Graphic by Emily Wang/The Gazelle  

The discussions on the Louvre and Guggenheim Abu Dhabi have so far been extremely convoluted and primarily focused on labor. There have already been two protests in the Guggenheim New York this year. Despite agreeing that the circumstances are extremely problematic, it is surprising that so many people jumped the gun to criticize labor conditions only because it is art institutions that are implicated. I sincerely doubt the backlash would have been this strong if we were talking only about UAE labor conditions. Thankfully, the protests and initiatives have brought about big changes in the Guggenheim’s labor standards, but I also sincerely think that many of these outbursts are derived from a much more cynical standpoint. The project was cast aside, portrayed as yet another extravagant construction made to publicize the United Arab Emirates and its development. I want to step away from the discussion of labor and take some time to explore the positive implications of these expansions.

When I first heard about the initiatives for Saadiyat, I quickly joined my friends in sneering at the idea. I was delighted at the prospect of these institutions being available to me, but it all seemed far too artificial and bizarre. I could only see it as a reverberation of the new art market spearheaded by Warhol, Koons and wealthy art consultants. The thought in itself was worthy of a Robert Hughes documentary. However, after living in Abu Dhabi for a year and learning more about the project — I was even present when the director of the Guggenheim was harshly confronted by a journalist at the Talking Art Series — I daresay that my outlook has changed significantly. I may still hate the art market, Warhol and Koons, but I will attempt to make a case for these museum branches.

The way I see it, the reason that this project has caused this much backlash is because a museum is a cultural entity. Creating such a strong, interdependent bond between cultural institutions and economic institutions is understandably dubious. It creates environments that care more about profit than about substance and quality of work. It creates an environment that easily censors art and denigrates the rights of the public in favor of big donations. This is perhaps why everyone has been so quick to criticize these expansion initiatives. The art market is increasingly driven by market demands that are in conflict with what the art world really needs. But it is too simple to think of these museum branches as just another misguided product of this relationship. Although the debate calls important issues to our attention, most of the argumentation surrounding the issue has been entirely disconnected from the purpose of this project: creating quality public spaces for art.

During the Guggenheim Talking Art Series at the Abu Dhabi Art fair last year, Monika Sosnowska discussed her large-scale sculptures and their relation to the war-torn Warsaw. She also showed one of the works that was purchased by the Guggenheim for the region. Large-scale is an understatement: The work filled an entire pavilion from corner to corner. Artists like her stand in the modern spirit of art-making today. This doesn’t mean that all artists make large-scale artworks, but this is something that needs to be considered. With the advent of installation art and large-scale art in the late 1950s, numerous pieces have been relegated to the lifespans of short exhibitions. They only remain in photographs and storage: The artists and art institutions have no space for them, or even their remnants. Museums and art institutions already have thousands of works that go unseen. The British Museum alone has approximately eight million works, and only a tiny percentage of them are shown. Another huge portion of work remains exclusively in private hands for decades. Creating museum branches is an excellent way to extend the lifespan of temporary works and to create public space for the innumerable works in the storages of huge institutions. It is a way to satisfy the demands of a growing number of works, and it provides the means to lengthen the public lifespan of art installations. This viewing public may be small, but that shouldn’t detract from the fact that Abu Dhabi’s investment is providing a space for the public display of important artworks.

The museums being built in Saadiyat are no doubt controversial, but there has been so much debate that we forgot to value the foremost quality of the museum: to make artwork accessible to the public. There is no doubt that there are many issues with respect to the construction of these museums, however the overarching effect of the initiative is undoubtedly positive. The massive structures of the two museums will provide a place for important works that need a space and an audience. It may not do much for the muddied art market, but it is certainly much better than displaying high-art vintage Porsches in fairs — I would recommend reading up on Art Dubai and Abu Dhabi Art. The expansion of the Guggenheim brand is concomitant with the growing art world and an excellent solution to the problem of art surplus. It is also infinitely better than the alternative forms of art display currently available in the country. And although the history of the UAE and its artificial islands didn’t really help the public reception of the concept, there is really nothing better than providing more quality public institutions for art. I would hate to be this optimistic, but the more education and public exposure is given to art, the more the economic underpinning of these projects can subside in favor of their cultural contributions. For now, it may only be a convenient way to import culture into a young country, but ultimately, it is an initiative that will increase art viewership and provide excellent spaces for work and cultural education. I can only hope that the initiatives to improve conditions on the island will bring about real change, and I stand optimistic about the endeavor and its contribution to the cultural landscape of the Gulf and the art world as a whole. Agustina Zegers is a contributing writer. Email her at opinion@thegazelle.org.

posts.markdown:
• Food Delivery
  • Damage Control
  • Campus Contacts
  • Beauty and Wellness

Lebanese

Try Mora for great, cheap lebanese and no delivery fee! Alternatively, Maroosh is an NYUAD classic. Call at 02 643 0525.

Afghani

For the highly praised Nolu Downtown, you can call at 02 644 1516.

Thai

Call Lemongrass at 02 677 0100. Alternatively, Stars & Cloves has spring rolls and fried rice to order at 02 5517227.

Sushi

One of the few sushi places that delivers to Saadiyat, Sushi Central is just a phone call away at 04 4409322, ext. 124.

Egyptian

Try something different with Altekia at 02 6786788.

Indian

Need your butter chicken fix? Call Al Ekram at 02 639 8000 and the comfort will come to you. Minimum delivery 150dhs. Also, more Indian food at Kababs & Kurries at 02 628 2522.

Saj

Zaatar, labneh, meat - your choice. Call Saj Hut at 02 6216217.

Burgers

Burger Bureau at 02 5641090. Prices hover around 30 AED. You'll find a veggie option and shakes at Burger Fuel - just dial 02 6738779.

Pizza

For when you're sick of Pizza Hut, call 800 Pizza at 800 74992. Or check out Il Forno, which has a large variety of options for toppings. Plus, garlic bread. Call at 04 4409322, ext. 189.

Deli Food

Bloomsbury's at 02 4914537 will get you croissants, breakfast platters and some cheaper sandwich options. Ortego's Deli has some fare with an Asian twist. Call at 02 6770740. Dessert: Wafflemeister at 02 6417949 offers toppings like chocolate, strawberries and marshmallows.

2 a.m. food

In a finals week spiral and looking for something to get you through it? Or do you just really like fried chicken? Call KFC at 600 522252. If you're in the mood for something else, try Pizza Hut at 600 569999. Numbers that every NYUAD student should have.

What it is

Dropped your phone? Spilled your midnight latte on your laptop? Have no fear, there’s somewhere on Hamdan that can help you out.

Medical services

Need a typhoid vaccine for a trip? Will Health and Wellness not fill your prescription anymore? New Medical Center takes our insurance. NMC Hospital: 02 633 2255 NMC pharmacy: 02 617 9820

Travel troubles

Are you lost at the airport? Flight delayed for a week? Call the NYUAD immigration team: 971 50 642 3212

Citibank

Wondering where your stipend went? Forgot your personal pin? For Citibank help call: 971 600 5 41114

Cabs

Save these numbers for cab service in Abu Dhabi and Dubai. Both have options for women’s only taxis! Call 600535353 for Abu Dhabi and 04 2080000 for Dubai.

Off-campus dry-cleaning

If you're dry-cleaning in a rush, there’s a place at the St Regis, Jeeves Dry Cleaning. Open 8:00am-11:00pm daily. Call 050 668 1167.

Parents visiting

If you have family coming and have no idea where to take them, think about a desert safari? One reliable company is Green Land Tourism at 055 4999 028 — join GroupOn first, though. There's most likely a deal.

posts.title: Misconduct in Voting During Special Session General Assembly
posts.markdown: Graphic by Mariko Kuroda/The Gazelle Editor’s note: The Gazelle has allowed the source in this article to remain anonymous due to the sensitivity of the findings and respect for the students involved. However, the source is willing to speak privately to administration if investigations are undertaken. The Gazelle has been able to verify this evidence with another source, who did not wish to be cited in the article. New claims have revealed misconduct in voting procedure during the special session General Assembly, of April 22, that voted against the motion to allow students on leave of absence to run in Student Government elections. During the special session GA, a group of nine voters had gathered at the Marketplace to watch the livestream on one student’s Google Hangouts account and submit their votes. The students sharing the account voted against the motion by submitting their votes via email. In accordance with Student Government procedure, virtual votes can only be counted if the sender was actively participating on the livestream — meaning they had been watching the video of the GA and paying attention to its procedures. The group had been sharing the Google Hangout on one computer, and their presence had not been verified on-screen; however, the group all testified to having actively participated by signing a Student Government form after the GA ended. Student Government released a report that included these signatures. Some members of the community raised doubts over whether the group had all been present in the GA, and whether their votes should be counted. After the Student Government elections, the Executive Board amended voting procedure so that all students livestreaming a GA must use their own Google Hangouts account. A source has recently come forward saying that the majority of these signatures were forged by a student and member of the voter group. The source was also told, by one of the nine students, that not all the voters in the Marketplace were actively participating on the livestream. “[The student] told me that not everyone was in the Marketplace watching with [them],” said the source. The source later spoke again with the student to check these allegations. “I asked… and [they] said no. I asked specifically, was everyone in the Marketplace, and [they] said no. [They] later said everyone might have not have been there but hanging around,” said the source. The source also said that two members of the Google Hangout group had personally admitted to them that not all of the signatures on the form were authentic. “[They] was unable to find everyone or get everyone to sign for themselves so [they] signed on behalf of people. [They] never told me a specific number, [they] told [someone else] that three people signed,” said the source. The source also added that they had been made aware, through conversations with those involved, that the presidential candidate in the group had known about this misconduct. The presidential candidate had been encouraged to come forward, but had not. The Gazelle approached the presidential candidate, who chose not to comment. The student signature collector denied the allegations. Zoe Hu and Joey Bui are editors in chief. Email them at feedback@gzl.me.

posts.title: Hassan Syed
posts.markdown:
Hassan Syed was unavailable for interview at time of publication.

The role of the Senator of the Student Government is to liaise with representatives from various entities within the UAE and the GNU regarding the interests of students of NYU Abu Dhabi. Having been born and raised in the Emirates to Pakistani and Emirati parents, I have at times experienced both the life of an expatriate and that of a UAE national. As such, I believe I’m well suited for the role of Senator as I can immerse myself in the local culture and can effectively advocate the interests of students and the NYUAD community. If elected, I aspire to initiate a conference for various Student Governments within the UAE, hosted by NYUAD, to be able to exchange ideas on student governance. This is in line with my vision of setting up NYU Abu Dhabi as the regional leader in Student Governance! I feel that my experience as the Operations intern at the Career Development Center has already allowed me to develop a strong interpersonal relationship with the people within the various departments that are key to ensuring that the Senator can perform his duties as necessary. If you catch me around, ask me about my plans for the Student Government!

posts.title: ARTIST: PRANAV MEHTA
posts.markdown:
Freshman Pranav Mehta is an engineering major who writes poetry about seemingly mundane things. His work doesn't conform to any particular style, but he makes sure to hide easter eggs in his poems every now and then. In his featured poem, Cotton clone, Mehta writes about a lost object lurking in laundry rooms.   If you’d like to listen to read more of Pranav's work, check out his website. To learn more about his work as an artist, listen to the podcast below.   To learn more about his work as an artist, listen to the podcast below.

Podcast (creative): Play in new window | Download

Subscribe: iTunes | RSS

 

Cotton clone

Twenty one days and thirty

strangers later, the

limonene-laced tang that hangs in

this theatre of thread, binds,

unwinds and rewinds

like an itchy insecurity

dignifying dread.

Stitch for stitch, these

tendons tensed on

ankles, toes and false

pretence. Binary births

are bonds of blood, but

we are stitch-fixed sheaths

that endure sweat, grime

and the double-timed rhythm of soles

in symphony.

We are cosy in cleats,

SPF-complete exoskeletons,

basking in the fabric froth of

rinse, spin, wring, repeat.

And yet, twenty one

days and thirty strangers

ago, swimming in a

whirlpool of

detergent-determined broth,

in a world of

dichotomous diversity,

twin togetherness,

distinct dualities,

how is it that

I was left

but you were all right?

You put the sorrow in sibilance.

 

Quarantined from mixed synthetics,

tumble-dried with shrunk aesthetics,

I lie among the slightly-linted

loose-fitting misfits.

I am a hole-turned-half,

umlaut in a paragraph,

resident of debris in a

perpetrated,

faithfully fractured

symmetry.

I miss the comforting

suffocation of your embrace

as we folded face-to face,

right-on-left-on-indistinguishable.

I miss hanging out in the sun

on the clothes-laden line that

dissolved the green grass from

the red-bled, alabaster linen laundry

in the pink of health.

I miss you, mirror me,

striped blue

facsimile.

Fill this void, forgotten friend

And put me back on feet again.

- Pranav Mehta

  Pranav Mehta’s work was selected to be published as part of an ongoing initiative, run by The Gazelle’s Creative Desk, to create a space for student artwork. The Creative Desk publishes works selected by a rotating panel. We are looking for prose, poetry, photography, film, visual arts, music and more. Send your creative work to isabellaperalta@nyu.edu. Submissions are accepted on a rolling basis. This week’s artwork was selected by creative editor Isabella Peralta. Email her at feedback@thegazelle.org.

posts.title: Andres Rodriguez
posts.markdown:
After fencing his way through high school and becoming part of the national fencing team in San José, Costa Rica, Andres Rodriguez’s new target is the student government.

Rodriguez, who was originally born in Mexico, travelled to many places such as Sudan, Nicaragua, Cuba and France. He grew up in Costa Rica where he attended high school before moving to NYUAD.

He once participated in the fencing youth world cup in Arizona and the Central American Championship in Nicaragua. Through participating in athletic SIGs, he has continued his passion for fencing.

Rodriguez also aspires to be a part of the student government at NYUAD. He has worked with the parliamentary advisory board and attended general assemblies to keep up with the university’s affairs.

“Working with [the parliamentary advisory board] really taught me a lot in terms of how the student government is run, how decisions are made and the needs of students,” Rodriguez said.

If elected, Rodriguez seeks to work closely with the staff and groups within the student body, such as the technology group to create an app for the bus schedule, and to connect the students more to the Abu Dhabi community.

posts.title: Andres Rodriguez
posts.markdown:
The past student government did a very good job at legitimizing itself both in front of the administration and the student body. As vice president, I hope to build on that legitimacy aiming to create a student government that addresses the needs of students and provides a voice for students to the administration and community. I along the future student government wish to keep promoting campaigns that facilitate the students' involvement in the Abu Dhabi community, community service programs and environmental efforts.

After working in the parliamentary advisory board I have also realized a want for increase transparency in the decision making of the government and its committees and would thus make it a priority to increase communications with interested students as to how and why decisions are made at the government level and staff level if and when possible.

posts.title: Geo Kamus
posts.markdown:
It may be hard to locate Geo Kamus on a weekend in Abu Dhabi. He could be swimming at an open pool night, skydiving indoors or mastering his Argentine Tango. But Kamus doesn't just welcome new experiences, he engages other students in the process with his passion for connecting students with one another and with opportunities on campus that align with their interests. Kamus won’t simply tell you about the time he went white water rafting. Instead, he will give you the pamphlet, directions and gear to try it out yourself.

“Those sorts of informal activities facilitate conversations,” Kamus said. “It’s always interesting to see people’s different perspectives on these cultural activities and I think that in itself is a learning experience in what brings people together.”

This nature of connectivity can be attributed to Kamus’ global upbringing, which brought him from the Philippines to Indonesia, and now, to Abu Dhabi.

“I can say now an international education gives whole new perspective on things,” Kamus said, describing how the lessons he has learned in academia and culture around the world never remain in one place. He carries these experiences with him and integrates them into any new learning environment.

Kamus believes this spirit of bringing people together and inspiring interaction is important for a senator. He sees connecting people, organizations and administration within the university as a way to eliminate the inefficiencies of multiple people trying to accomplish the same goal.

posts.title: Angelina Micha Djaja
posts.markdown:
You may find Angelina Micha Djaja around the NYUAD campus sporting a shirt patterned with elephants, large thick-rimmed glasses and with a viola in tow. The product of an art school in Toronto, Djaja exudes creativity. Her decision to run for treasurer at first seems unusual for someone who loves to read books, perform music and indulge in her artistic side. But this individuality actually aligns with her interest in pursing a position rooted in structure and planning. In addition to having a knack for numbers and organization, Djaja is detail-oriented and enjoys coordinating activities.

“Allotting the budget means you will automatically be involved with event planning,” Djaja said. “That is another aspect of the position that I was interested in.”

In the past, she has organized benefit concerts and coffee houses to raise money for organizations like Free the Children as the leader of the Social Justice Club at her school. One of her most rewarding experiences involved fundraising for the Artbound initiative, which builds sustainable educational infrastructure in developing countries.

But, Djaja has demonstrated the ability to keep track of money well since before she got involved with event management.

“My parents told always told me that I would notice anytime they would take something from me,” Djaja said. “If someone borrowed money from me, I would never forget."

This sharp attention to detail and a commitment to transparency in matters of money and government are what motivated Djaja to run for treasurer.

In addition to having a knack for numbers and organization, Djaja is detail-oriented and enjoys coordinating activities.

“Allotting the budget means you will automatically be involved with event planning,” Djaja said. “That is another aspect of the position that I was interested in.”

In the past, she has organized benefit concerts and coffee houses to raise money for organizations like Free the Children as the leader of the Social Justice Club at her school. One of her most rewarding experiences involved fundraising for the Artbound initiative, which builds sustainable educational infrastructure in developing countries.

But, Djaja has demonstrated the ability to keep track of money well since before she got involved with event management.

“My parents told always told me that I would notice anytime they would take something from me,” Djaja said. “If someone borrowed money from me, I would never forget."

This sharp attention to detail and a commitment to transparency in matters of money and government are what motivated Djaja to run for treasurer.

posts.title: Massimiliano Valli
posts.markdown:
Massimiliano Valli was 11 years old when his parents led him to a gathering of 4,000 people on the streets of Kyrgyzstan to witness the beginning of the Tulip Revolution. Watching the storming of the Kyrgyz White House and the deposing of President Askar Akayev marked the beginning of Valli’s political aspirations.

Today at NYUAD, he is the only freshman running for president and is already the president of the Economics and Finance Club.

The Tulip Revolution, he said, “made [him] think of the role of government in society … and how it should help citizens with their quality of life.”

At NYUAD, he wants to increase transparency in government, give students a voice in the creation of the Saadiyat Campus and install a bike share system.

On his candidate’s weekend, Valli was impressed by the enormous input the NYUAD students can have on the university. In order to unify the students at NYUAD, he hopes to “set a precedent and traditions, drawing ideas from the students.”

In his spare time he jogs on the Corniche, grabs saaj-to-go and plays basketball and volleyball. He likes to read books on politics and economics for pleasure, including a few philosophy books every now and then. His focus, however, is on expanding the idealistic vision of NYUAD.

“I want to go into policy making to be able to change people’s lives on a large scale,” Valli said. “Teachers abide by guidelines, I want to set those guidelines.”

posts.title: Massimiliano Valli
posts.markdown: The President of Student Government has a crucial role in guiding NYU Abu Dhabi through these formative years. Raising and maintaining high standards will thus be essential in developing a Student Government that not only helps and represents the current Student Body but will also serve similar functions for future students. In order to accomplish this, as president, I promise to enhance NYU Abu Dhabi’s “eco-friendly” capacity by establishing a bike system and make government more transparent by reforming the committee system and provide more thorough minutes. I promise to assist in developing and fostering NYUAD’s intellectual community by establishing a system (similar to Dartmouth’s) through which students can take professors out past the confines of Sama Tower and DTC. I believe in keeping the Student Body not only informed but also a part of the policy discussion at the school. This includes having the administration give a presentation on Saadiyat Island and working with the office of the Provost to improve NYUAD’s rudimentary curriculum. Communication is key for every leader, and I promise to bring innovative ideas and to listen to you. I would be honored to serve you as President of the Student Government.

posts.title: Corey Meyer
posts.markdown:
A biter, a runner, a leader, a future foreign policy maker and a current sophomore candidate for vice president in the Student Government, Corey Meyer easily combines a well-balanced and confident appearance with an adventurous sparkle in his eyes.

Inspired by his classmate’s screams, “It’s just around the corner!” he successfully completed Dead to Red relay in Jordan last year. His dream is to run marathons on each of the continents, including the one along the Great Wall of China.

The opportunity that in many ways shaped his NYUAD experience so far is an internship position in the Department of Global Education, last year as UAE and Regional Travel Intern and this year as Chief Ambassador to NYU New York Students. Just recently, Meyer attended a relationship formation meeting between the UAE National Center for Documentation and Research and NYUAD’s Department of Global education, which he believes can potentially result in great opportunities for the NYUAD students to research and to deepen their understanding of UAE history.

After serving as president of his high school back home in Columbus, Ohio, running for the vice president at NYUAD seems like a natural decision for Meyer. He observed student government weekly assemblies for the past two years and was a collected member of the Honor Code Committee.

Meyer is not just a political science student who admires John F. Kennedy and dreams of working in the U.S. Department of State on policy making and shaping international relations. He is also an active leader of the pre-law, first aid and advocacy student interest groups.

For Meyer, life is an unpredictable marathon with challenging hurdles that he is eager to overcome. He said it took him getting thrown out of preschool multiple times for biting his peers, as well as facing a fear of heights, to get this far. Now he is getting ready for his future plans that seem to be seen just around the corner: participation in the Hult Challenge Competition and fulfilling his collection with the marathon in Cyprus.

posts.title: Corey Meyer
posts.markdown: It would be my sincere honor to serve you as Vice President of Student Government. I bring my experiences as a former Student Body President, an active attendee of General Assembly meetings, and a SIG leader. As your Vice President I would focus on improving the student funding process through increased access for SIG reimbursement. Furthermore, over the next several semesters we need to reorient planning to focus on the upcoming transition to Saadiyat Island. This means an increased focus on sustainability and transferability of all Student Government services and programs for future students. Today, the maintenance of these services present challenges in upkeep that must be met with careful decisions to ensure the survival of these services. Specifically, a system for maintaining equipment in the student lounge needs to be designed to prevent damage and loss. Outside the realm of tangible services, I would continue the tradition of heavy student involvement in the crafting and reform of academic and student life policy by ensuring all students have a voice in the policy design process. I am excited for the possibility to serve you and our community. I hope I can count on your support.

posts.title: Leah Reynolds
posts.markdown:
Leah Reynolds is always thinking about how to unify people. She brings students together as a leader in various SIGs and NYUAD Spiritual Life. Before finals, bringing food and pillows to crowded study rooms is her mark of camaraderie. From organizing Christian Fellowship events, Reynolds has connected people from all walks of life in the wider Abu Dhabi community. Her candidate platform is focused on strengthening the NYUAD community, especially for incoming classes and for students studying abroad.

At the same time, Reynolds is driven by the individuals around her. Of the NYUAD community, she is convinced that each person has an interesting story to tell and a talent to be revealed. She wants to create more opportunities for NYUAD students to tell their stories and show their abilities, to “tap into the things that make people special,” she said. When she worked on a committee to discuss school values, Reynolds emphasized the importance of representing the great differences of this diverse community.

Beyond achievements on paper, Reynold’s inclination toward actively assembling students while still seeing each person as an individual, suggests the kind of student government president she hopes to be. Reynolds is the person that connects people and gives them opportunities. She is also the kind of person offering Sweethearts to her visitors and even more when they leave to bring them back for their roommates.

posts.title: Leah Reynolds
posts.markdown: One thing I’ve learned as part of NYUAD’s inaugural class is that we’re a community of people who can cast a vision and build great things where they didn’t exist before. I’ve also found that my strength in this entrepreneurial process lies in solidifying existing structures, and in refining and organizing what’s been built. In the past two years I’ve co-lead SIGs, interned on campus, and served on committees to discuss issues like the the Honor Code. Through this I’ve gained the experience and perspective needed to work efficiently and productively for our community. By staying in Abu Dhabi, I’ve had the privilege of connecting deeply to both our university community and the city we live in. During the next year each NYUAD class will crave stability in different ways. Juniors need clear communication regarding capstones and commencement so we can leave a worthwhile legacy. Sophomores, and all those returning from study abroad, need smooth transitions that maintain a sense of community. Freshman need to be fully integrated into that community and equipped for leadership roles. Previous student governments have built a solid foundation, and I’d like to lead as president in fulfilling our responsibility to build upon it well.

posts.title: Andrew Pitts
posts.markdown:
Andrew Pitts, a junior from Philadelphia, is clear about what he hopes to see in the coming year: more integration between the classes. In his bid for presidency of the Student Government, he intends to make it part of his plan to “revolutionize the education.” Events where the students can mingle is not enough, and he wants to see integration on a deeper level and inside the classrooms.

“It dismayed me,” Pitts said. “There were no freshmen in my J-Term class.”

Of all the classes Pitts is taking this semester, he has only one class with a freshman. In such a small community, it is possible for everyone to know everyone which, as Pitts pointed out, is a blessing and a curse.

He compares his experience in NYUAD’s community to his semester abroad at NYU New York, where he struggled to meet people. While he enjoyed spending time with his younger sister, a freshman at the New York campus, he found it difficult to integrate into the community and has since decided to spend the remainder of his undergraduate career in Abu Dhabi.

As one of the few students who did not sign the Student Government Constitution when it was first created, Pitts acknowledged his tendency to be critical. He believes that there is always room for dissent and criticism. Ultimately, Pitts believes that Student Government should foster an environment that gets all the students involved.

posts.title: Andrew Pitts
posts.markdown:
It’s a hard thing to run for office. You have to put yourself out there. Here I am: My name is Andrew, I’m a junior, a philosophy and literature major, and the colour of my beard does not match the colour of my hair. For me, this school is everything. If I hadn’t come to NYUAD I have no idea what I would have done. I’ll go right out there and say it: This school has come a long way, in three short years we have gone from being nothing to a real living and breathing community. However, that journey is far from over. I truly believe that NYUAD has the potential to revolutionize the way education is viewed throughout the world.

However, while ‘well begun is half-way done’ we still have so much left to do. We have a choice before us, will this NYU Abu Dhabi experiment be looked back on as founded with the right intentions but never actualized, or will people look back and only see our success. Right now, complacency is the enemy we have to continue striving forward in order for the NYU Abu Dhabi experiment to change the world.

posts.title: Alex Nyikos
posts.markdown:
Alex Nyikos is an anomaly. He lives in modern day society as a busy and socially active university student, yet he does not own a cell phone.

“I had a phone for all of three months in my life,” Nyikos admits. “I used it three times, and since lost it and can’t find it.”

While most of us see our phone as an additional appendage, Nyikos asserts that the latest iPhone is not necessary to maintain a tight-knit group of friends.

“Here, we all live in the same building,” he explained. “It’s easy enough to bump into someone and connect with them. I prefer doing that.”

Nyikos’s social circle is a result of not only the serendipity of the Sama run-ins, but also his patience and dedication to relationships.

“I like to follow up with people,” he said. “So if I meet them, it’s not like I meet them once and never see them for the rest of the semester.”

This type of persistence, difficult to attain as part of university social life, prevails in Nyikos’s hobbies as well – whether it be debate, piano or a game of Halo with friends. A fan of astronomy, Nyikos was in charge of the Observatory at his high school and worked a job at McDonald’s for a summer to earn enough money to buy his own telescope.

Nyikos plans to apply the same kind of determination to student government.

“I’m kind of tenacious with things,” he said. “If I start doing something, I like to see it through. I don’t like to leave those things half-done.”

posts.title: Alex Nyikos
posts.markdown: This year will be a very important and transitional one for our university and student government. Preparations for the move to the Saadiyat Island campus will be intensifying, and it will be very important for us as a student body to ensure that our collective voice is heard in the planning process. This year, we will have the truly unique opportunity to begin making the new campus our own. The last student government was responsible for the creation of the SIG funding structure, the Safe Space Policy, the Honor Code, and many other policies that help make our student experience what it is. The next government will have to ensure the sustainability of these structures in the context of a full campus; we will need to guarantee that funding structures are as efficient and responsive as possible. In the case of SIGs, this could be done by boosting the hours available to exchange funds and allowing leftover funds for individual SIGs to roll over to future semesters, for example. I am running for student body president with the hope that you will entrust me with the responsibility and privilege to represent you through this very exciting period for our university.

posts.title: Irene Pañeda
posts.markdown:
Irene Pañeda is as serious about keeping the junior class connected — the majority being abroad — as she is about uniting the diverse peoples and countries of the world. She interweaves the narrative of interconnectedness and understanding by students, citizens and ultimately the human race in her pursuits. She sees and accepts people as citizens of the world.

“The characters are all my friends, they are all imperfect,” Irene said of Anton Chekov’s “Uncle Vanya,” her favorite play.

Pañeda studied abroad in New York City at the Playwrights Horizon Theater School at NYU’s Tisch School of the Arts. She loved the tight, communal feel of the group which reminded her of the NYUAD community.

Pañeda also has a strong passion for interdisciplinary learning. She is a double major in politics and theatre, and she is completing her capstone in political economy. Her capstone concentrates on the reasons for international cooperation through economic causation. Much unlike the characters in “Uncle Vanya,” Pañeda is never preoccupied with imperfection; she believes it is the foundation of international understanding. She is driven and open to the challenges that our generation will face, including her optimistic belief that the current economic crisis will further unite the world community.

Pañeda aspires to work with the European Union or another international organization after she graduates. An oasis of wisdom in the desert, Pañeda embodies the idea that, as said by Chekov, “the world perishes not from bandits and fires, but from hatred, hostility, and all these petty squabbles.”

Pañeda aspires to work with the European Union or another international organization after she graduates. An oasis of wisdom in the desert, Pañeda embodies the idea that, as said by Chekov, “the world perishes not from bandits and fires, but from hatred, hostility, and all these petty squabbles.”

posts.title: Morgante Pell
posts.markdown:
Vermont-native Morgante Pell proves that a political degree is not a requirement to demonstrate your passion for student government. As a computer science and economics double major, Pell is chairman of the Research and Development committee. His achievements include developing a school account with Spotify, an online music application that streams music, available in the Campus Lounge.

As an alternate senator candidate, Pell hopes to continue his work towards identifying areas of improvement within the student body and applying his technical knowledge to alleviate problems.

“I believe very strongly in humanitarian technology,” Pell said. “Bill Gates is a huge humanitarian. Technology is a way of looking at problems — I would hesitate to use the word technology. I should say, I look at things through models and systems.”

While he is only halfway into his freshman year, Pell is already committed to using his knowledge of technology and social networks to better the campus community. Through creating a simplified version of a social network based on the student population, Pell can see how altering situations can affect student relationships.

“Maybe we can look at how doing Marhaba with upperclassmen here might increase cross-class collaboration,” he proposed.

As alternate senator, Pell hopes to alleviate the stress involved in running a SIG with the development of an attendance tracker application. He will also advocate for a SIG of the month program to acknowledge the variety of groups operating on campus.

Pell’s commitment to student government will continue no matter the results of the polls.

“I want to make sure we are going in a good direction — staying true to our values as NYUAD, and supporting students and student government,” he said. “Whether I am elected or not, that won’t change. I’ll be going to General Assemblies, and I’ll still be advocating.”

posts.title: Otto Kakhidze
posts.markdown:
On an archeological excavation near the border between Armenia and Georgia, presidential candidate Otto Kakhidze recalled, with sheer fervor, excavating two teeth of a medieval pig.

Kakhidze’s intellectual curiosities manifest in his excavations with the National Museum of Georgia and also permeate his social interactions. He spent nights of his freshman Marhaba week caught up in philosophical debates with his new peers. It is difficult to find students whose academic drive stems from a genuine love for learning; this special quality exists in Kakhidze — a true academic.

But many NYUAD students are privy to the other sides of Kakhidze’s multifaceted character. He is a published poet, equestrian, capoeirista, hiker and rugby player. His extensive interests and passion for cultures are what make him approachable. He was active in student government as School Prefect in Scotland and as class representative last year. In Georgia, he founded the local chapter of the European Youth Parliament, which gave him the opportunity to dance the chicken dance alongside former French President, Nicolas Sarkozy. Kakhidze’s achievements as a leader are not going unrecognized, as he will receive the prestigious “Duke of Edinburgh’s International Award” this summer.

Kakhidze prides himself in managing to entrench a core universal value in his ever-evolving psyche — that of the responsibility to “love every human being.” This Georgian man has a lot of love to give, and with his unrelenting perseverance and sincerity, Kakhidze continues to let this value system persist in the unique community that is NYUAD. And despite all that Kakhidze has accomplished, his biggest achievement may be his ability to make others laugh.

posts.title: Clara Correia
posts.markdown:
When 18-year-old Brazil native Clara Correia began her college career at NYUAD she had the intentions of studying political science. But, after taking Nathalie Peutz’s “Anthropology and the Arab World” course, she was inspired to focus on humanitarianism and peace resolutions around the world.

Last semester Correia helped organize “Peace One Day” to commemorate the United Nation’s International Day of Peace on September 21. Additionally, she is working to create a Peace and Conflict SIG with freshman Louis Plottel.

“Part of the purpose is to create this platform where we can foster cultural understanding and enhance knowledge about the conflicts that are going on around the world,” Correia explained.

Correia is making sure that the Peace and Conflict SIG has the necessary foundations needed to sustain its development for the ongoing years by contacting professors and faculty members who could generate greater interest for a successful network.

As an alternate senator candidate, Correia would like to focus her efforts on creating a sustainable leadership transferral system for SIGs.

“I realized because of the nature of the university where students go away, especially with the juniors who started a lot of the SIGs, there are some issues with transferring positions and ensuring that the SIG continues,” she said.

The NYUAD freshman would also like to improve communication and transparency among SIG leaders and Student Government. In her past experience working on her student government at her former school in Hong Kong, she was part of a movement to create YouTube videos to inform students of the latest news and decisions to increase transparency.

Ultimately, Correia would like to strengthen the SIGs before Saadiyat, to ensure the establishment and continuity of the program.

posts.title: Veronica Houk
posts.markdown:
Veronica Houk, the unopposed candidate running for student government secretary, loves to cook. With the vegan-vegetarian advocacy SIG Veggie Might, which she helped to start, Houk has worked on spreading vegan awareness through cooking.

“We did a huge vegan thanksgiving last semester that was the shamble-iest but the most beautiful thing ever – you didn’t think you could put so much food in a blender, but we made it happen,” Houk said.

A vegan since her freshman year of high school, Houk loves to share the vegan point of view, whether through screening themed documentaries or baking vegan cupcakes.

“This school is very conducive to vegetarianism, and it seems like a lot of the students are interested and open-minded about it,” she said. “I’m really grateful for that.”

Linked with her veganism is a passion for the environment. And she hopes to develop this passion through the environment multidisciplinary concentration: “I find global warming and climate change really interesting. It almost feels irresponsible not to do anything,” Houk said.

Between Veggie Might and student government, she views the two sides complimentary but very separate forms of leadership.

A freshman, Houk already has strongly rooted herself in the NYUAD community through her work as a Global Education intern and as a member of the Hall Council. Now, as the only student running for secretary, she is looking forward to formalizing structures to improve efficiency of projects for the student government.

“I think [SG] is a way for the administration and students to bridge the divide and to create a dialogue in which you can actually change the policy, change the way things are set up,” she said. “We’re so young, we can be whoever we want to be.”

Houk plans on keeping her roles with Veggie Might and student government separate. But with her on board, you never know when vegan cupcakes may show up.

posts.markdown:
Due to NYUAD’s youth and developing character, its Student Government has the heightened opportunity and responsibility to influence the school’s growth, strength, and integrity. The University’s previous student administrations made commitments to a democratic representation of the student body and its wishes, the establishment of Student Government’s roles and responsibilities, and open communication throughout the Global Network University. I am dedicated not only to continuing these legacies but also to creating a unified framework for traditions, procedures, and collaborations within the University. This structure will provide precedent for future governments as well as foster Student Governments based on partnership rather than individuals or discrete committees and boards.

As Secretary, I will contribute to a proactive, forthright leadership that will cultivate an environment in which students continue to have a voice in policy, events, and student life. I invite the NYUAD student body to join me in this vision.

posts.title: Angela Ortega Pastor
posts.markdown:
Despite being only in her second semester at NYUAD, Angela Ortega Pastor can say with conviction that her field of study is economics. The current treasurer for the economics and finance SIG, Pastor thrives on sharing her passion for economics with her friends beyond academics.

“It provides a different way of looking at economics,” she said.

As treasurer, Pastor has worked on developing budgets with the student government for the past six months. Her goal is to take everything she has learned at the SIG level and to apply herself to the student government, which she believes is vital for nurturing student life.

“It’s a really great intermediary between the management and the student body and its, if it does a good job it will be able to represent well what the students want this university to be,” she said.

Pastor draws on the political and economic troubles in her home country of Spain to reflect on the importance of a well-run and well-structured government.

“Politicians shouldn’t just be politicians, but experts on things like economics,” she said. “Everyone has the opportunity to explore and to expand on their own interests and I think there should be a fair distribution, but we also need to be rational and realistic.”

When she is not busy with the economics and finance SIG, Pastor spends her free time exploring Abu Dhabi by foot, whether to find Afghan bread and chai tea or to watch the sunset from the Corniche with her roommates. And whenever her home team, Real Madrid, has a big match, Pastor will certainly be watching.

posts.title: Students, faculty dine their way through Abu Dhabi
posts.markdown: Photo credit: Courtesy of Flavors of Abu Dhabi It’s a Wednesday evening and you are meeting with a group of students over dinner to sample a new cuisine. Maybe tonight is Mexican food and you will enjoy fresh guacamole prepared right at your table. Maybe you will sit in a circle and scoop up Ethiopian stews with pieces of bread, or reminisce in New York hamburger culture at the Abu Dhabi Shake Shack.   Flavors of Abu Dhabi is a bi-monthly program that takes groups of students out to explore a variety of ethnic restaurants around the city. The program launched early last semester with a visit to a Mongolian Hot Pot. Since then, there have been 10 outings with a new type of cuisine each time.   Khulood Al Atiyat, Assistant Director of Student Life, runs the program though the Office of Intercultural Affairs and explained that the idea originated as a personal quest when she first moved to Abu Dhabi.   “I love food and I love trying authentic restaurants,” Al Atiyat said. “When it comes to food, I can’t be biased towards any one kind – I can’t choose a favorite.”   Al Atiyat adheres to a number of criteria when selecting a restaurant for the program. She chooses restaurants that represent the different nationalities at NYUAD.   Part of the program’s goal is to introduce students to restaurants in the hopes that they will return to their favorites. Al Atiyat tries to keep the price range within the means of a student budget. She has high standards when it comes to dining and almost always goes to the restaurant to review the new establishment before taking the students. “My reputation is at stake,” she said. “If I recommend a restaurant, it has to be good.”   Freshman Jiwon Shin highly recommends Flavors of Abu Dhabi. In fact, she has attended almost every restaurant outing.   “I like the program because it gives the students the opportunity to experience different cultures,” Shin said, identifying the Saudi Kitchen as her preferred restaurant.   Shin pointed out that experiencing new cultures often involves experimenting with the unusual or unexpected; the strangest thing she has tried was a raw meat dish at an Ethiopian restaurant. She said it was quite good, and that she was glad she tasted the dish.   Al Atiyat hopes that students will begin to take a leading role with Flavors of Abu Dhabi, especially as she wants to expand the project to include going out for breakfast next semester. She said she is looking for a few students to help research and discover restaurants, plan the menus and organize the outings.   Flavors of Abu Dhabi will be visiting a Korean restaurant sometime within the coming weeks. The time and place of each outing will be announced on the Student Portal. Those interested in attending the next outing can contact her at Al Atiyat kaa310@nyu.edu. Clare Hennig is features editor. Email her at thegazelle.org@gmail.com.

It’s a Wednesday evening and you are meeting with a group of students over dinner to sample a new cuisine. Maybe tonight is Mexican food and you will enjoy fresh guacamole prepared right at your table. Maybe you will sit in a circle and scoop up Ethiopian stews with pieces of bread, or reminisce in New York hamburger culture at the Abu Dhabi Shake Shack.

 

Flavors of Abu Dhabi is a bi-monthly program that takes groups of students out to explore a variety of ethnic restaurants around the city. The program launched early last semester with a visit to a Mongolian Hot Pot. Since then, there have been 10 outings with a new type of cuisine each time.

 

Khulood Al Atiyat, Assistant Director of Student Life, runs the program though the Office of Intercultural Affairs and explained that the idea originated as a personal quest when she first moved to Abu Dhabi.

 

“I love food and I love trying authentic restaurants,” Al Atiyat said. “When it comes to food, I can’t be biased towards any one kind – I can’t choose a favorite.”

 

Al Atiyat adheres to a number of criteria when selecting a restaurant for the program. She chooses restaurants that represent the different nationalities at NYUAD.

 

Part of the program’s goal is to introduce students to restaurants in the hopes that they will return to their favorites. Al Atiyat tries to keep the price range within the means of a student budget. She has high standards when it comes to dining and almost always goes to the restaurant to review the new establishment before taking the students. “My reputation is at stake,” she said. “If I recommend a restaurant, it has to be good.”

 

Freshman Jiwon Shin highly recommends Flavors of Abu Dhabi. In fact, she has attended almost every restaurant outing.

posts.title: New exhibit honors old Abu Dhabi at Qasr al Hosn
posts.markdown: Photo credit: Courtesy of Nina Bayatti In the midst of tall towers and perfectly aligned palm trees along the super block lays Qasr al Hosn — a live exhibit of culture, tradition and history. Giant buildings jut out from behind, creating a modern backdrop to traditional huts inside the exhibit. A man clad in a traditional dress weaves shiny silver wires into the making of a fishnet, known as a gargour in the Emirati culture.   As Abu Dhabi grew both as a city and a population, what began as a watchtower expanded into a fortress and now a palace, known as Qasr al Hosn, meaning palace of the defense in Arabic. The palace is in the middle of the city and is both a reflection of the past as well as a celebration of Abu Dhabi's progress. Qasr al Hosn's humble beginnings originate from a centuries-old watchtower, constructed in 1761 on a patch of land where the Sheikh of the Bani Yas tribes discovered a fresh water oasis. Today, stalls of ceramic pottery, gold embroidered dresses and locally made artwork occupy the outdoor area. Men in kandoras sit on patches of sand as they use long pieces of wood and short, sharp knives to build the frame of dhow boats. They continue their work with little attention to the people perusing the stalls and stations. Families take their time browsing through the many exhibits, while giggling toddlers in miniature kandoras dart and weave between stalls. Some of the children linger by the camel-petting area, offering apple slices and other treats to their hump-backed friends. Freshman Nino Cricco attended the festival as part of a first-year programming event. “Living in Sama and being inside, you can get the sense that … there is nothing to do, there is no history, there is no culture,” Cricco said. “But there is. You just have to go out and find it.” In addition to the outdoor stations, the festival hosts a theatrical show explaining the creation of the United Arab Emirates. Photo credit: Courtesy of Nina Bayatti

In the midst of tall towers and perfectly aligned palm trees along the super block lays Qasr al Hosn — a live exhibit of culture, tradition and history. Giant buildings jut out from behind, creating a modern backdrop to traditional huts inside the exhibit. A man clad in a traditional dress weaves shiny silver wires into the making of a fishnet, known as a gargour in the Emirati culture.

 

As Abu Dhabi grew both as a city and a population, what began as a watchtower expanded into a fortress and now a palace, known as Qasr al Hosn, meaning palace of the defense in Arabic. The palace is in the middle of the city and is both a reflection of the past as well as a celebration of Abu Dhabi's progress. Qasr al Hosn's humble beginnings originate from a centuries-old watchtower, constructed in 1761 on a patch of land where the Sheikh of the Bani Yas tribes discovered a fresh water oasis. Today, stalls of ceramic pottery, gold embroidered dresses and locally made artwork occupy the outdoor area. Men in kandoras sit on patches of sand as they use long pieces of wood and short, sharp knives to build the frame of dhow boats. They continue their work with little attention to the people perusing the stalls and stations. Families take their time browsing through the many exhibits, while giggling toddlers in miniature kandoras dart and weave between stalls. Some of the children linger by the camel-petting area, offering apple slices and other treats to their hump-backed friends. Freshman Nino Cricco attended the festival as part of a first-year programming event. “Living in Sama and being inside, you can get the sense that … there is nothing to do, there is no history, there is no culture,” Cricco said. “But there is. posts.title: Sleepless students discuss coping methods for lack of rest
posts.markdown: Photo credit: Courtesy of Sala Shaker From the abundance of health advice students receive from parents, doctors and old episodes of “Barney & Friends,” we know that sleep is an important asset to the body and brain. The universal standard of eight hours per night is repeated in magazines, TV shows and the unsolicited life advice we hear at the family dinner table. But is this standard unrealistic? Has the bar been set too high? For many college students, a healthy night’s sleep is a concept rendered obsolete, much like the idea of free time or reading for pleasure. At NYUAD, schoolwork knocks sleep off the to-do list, demoting it to a status beneath assignment deadlines, projects and extracurriculars. Sophomore Noha Alfergani is the archetype of a busy college student. As a resident assistant and a Foundations of Science student majoring in engineering, Alfergani usually does not get more than three hours of sleep per night. “On a good night I’ll get five, and that happens only on weekends,” Alfergani said. “Even during the weekend, you have work, problem sets or a lab report.” Students commonly cope with sleep deprivation with caffeine and naps. But this could be detrimental to students’ health. “It is best to keep consistent sleep patterns,” said Lisa Young, a professor of Health and Nutrition at NYUNY. “And avoid beverages including coffee, caffeinated soft drinks and energy drinks.” Young believes that a better alternative to caffeine is something as simple as a bigger helping of food at dinner. Students can make up for an absence of sleep through larger portions and more calories. Alfergani, who has averaged three hours of sleep since the beginning of the semester, has become so used to this schedule that the concept of more sleep is strange and even unappealing. “If I sleep for more than eight hours, my back starts hurting and my bones get sore,” Alfergani said. “I’m not used to it.” But long stretches of being awake eventually do take effect. Alfergani was nonchalant and even good-humored as she recounted one instance of oversleeping for 15 hours. “I came back from the labs at six and decided to take a nap for 20 minutes. I slept at 6:30 p.m. and woke up at 8:00 a.m. the next day.” Nasser Isleem, an Arabic Professor at NYUAD, said he notices the effects of sleep-deprivation in class particularly, especially after students go on trips. “I once had a student who flew to Sri Lanka over the weekend, and that really caused a lot of sleep deprivation,” Isleem said. “Some of [the students], when they talk about their work, say that they stay up late and they have some sleep disorders. I relate that to the possibility of the course loads that they have, the events that they are required to go to — there are many demands that go on at Student Life here.” Regardless of their busy schedules, students are still required to participate and engage in class. “Nobody can hide in my class,” Isleem said. “Because of the fact that we have a small number of students, students are alert in class and I do require that students are kept awake.” Umair Saad, a sophomore engineering student, has also noticed the impact that a lack of sleep can have on daily life. “By Wednesday I’m just too tired,” he said. “Every class I go to I’m too tired, and my brain melts and I go crazy.” Saad believes that productivity can make all the difference for maintaining healthy sleep patters. “If you work on time and you get it done, then you can get enough sleep,” Saad said. “Most of the time we’re not completely devastated or destroyed from lack of sleep. It’s just that we’re tired in general.” Freshman James Smoley said he manages to get enough rest by adhering to a steady sleep schedule. “My bedtime is 9:30 p.m.,” Smoley said. “So even if I’m not looking at a clock, when it hits 9:30 p.m., I’m tired and I can’t focus. There’s no point in staying up.” Freshman Allen Magnusson, another FOS student, said he remains alert in class through a carefully planned regime of napping. “I’m a big proponent of napping,” Magnusson said. “So I have classes in the morning, and I’m sure to take a nap for about two hours afterwards, which leaves me feeling pretty refreshed.” Caffeine is a source of quick energy that helps keep many students moving. On difficult days, Saad drinks about four cups of tea and two cups of coffee. Despite these coping methods, after a long period of time losing sleep can have adverse effects on academics and social lives. “The exhaustion was impeding my ability to focus,” said freshman Megan Vincent, who has recently purchased a coffee maker for AED 50 from Al Safa. “Focusing becomes an issue when you lose a lot of sleep, and you’re also in an irritable mood.” Finding balance is not easy for students who continue to treat sleep deprivation with temporary solutions that specialists like Young advise students to avoid. Saad remembered a particularly tired day that epitomizes students in need of more hours of rest. “Once we were taking notes in class, and after we got home, my friend realized that her notes were literally just scribbles on a page,” he said. “They weren’t even words. Just scribbles.” Zoe Hu is deputy news editor. Email her at thegazelle.org@gmail.com.

posts.title: SIGs suffer as Student Government enforces new regulations on funding
posts.markdown: Photo credit: Nina Bayatti/The Gazelle Mariko Kuroda is a small girl with big dreams. A dainty force to be reckoned with, Kuroda has ambitious goals for the university. She plans to start the first ever handbell ensemble that NYUAD has ever seen. Handbells date back to the 17th century and consist of a group of musicians who ring bells with different tones. “I love the unity that handbells entail,” Kuroda said. “If one person in the group is missing, then the music crumbles. And if we’re not on beat and we’re not breathing together, then the music crumbles. I just want the NYUAD community to enjoy and appreciate and discover the beauty of handbells.” To do this, Kuroda has formed a handbell SIG, an idea suggested to her by Campus Life as the easiest way to approach receiving funding for resources. Yet, Kuroda has encountered many difficulties trying to finance her endeavor. A set of bronze handbells costs 14,000 U.S. dollars – a steep price that Student Government can’t afford. Kuroda is willing to settle for a 3,000-dollar set of handchimes. But even these, which greatly limit the volume and style of handbell music, were a struggle to procure. According to Kuroda, it took a month to hash out prices and negotiate with both the sellers and the Student Government, which includes the process of getting the SIG approved and revising its budget. Although Kuroda is now set on ordering the cheaper set, she is left with only two months of the school year to gather her seven-person ensemble and scrape together a performance. And even with the handchimes, Kuroda is lacking an integral part of music playing – the notes themselves. At the moment, her ensemble does not have any sheet music. Each sheet costs roughly five U.S. dollars, but Kuroda has been approved for enough sheet music for only one song. “My options now are to illegally download, or compose my own music,” Kuroda jokes, delicate fingers shoved into her inky mass of hair. She feels that the new status of her SIG poses a disadvantage. “If I had started in the fall, there would have been time for the SIG to grow,” she said. Like Kuroda, freshman Nino Cricco, a leader of the new visual arts SIG 1607 has experienced similar difficulties in terms of receiving funding as a new SIG this semester. “It’s hard considering that older SIGs get priority because they have a more established history of doing a good job,” said Cricco. “But I think [Student Government] is doing a good job of getting people to have realistic expectations and not just letting people spend tons of money on the most expensive pizza.” Cricco’s SIG had to make several cuts on art supplies, which are already expensive and scarce in Abu Dhabi. “It’s been hard adjusting our expectations, which were extremely unrealistic.” Cricco said, looking down to smile at his rubber flip-flops. “Extremely unrealistic.” But many pre-existing SIGs say that cutbacks have not noticeably impacted their SIGs’ day-to-day procedures. “We are pleased with the current situation of Blacksmith and [Abu Dhabi Campus Fellowship],” said junior Stephen Underwood of the two SIGS he is involved with. He is leader of Blacksmith, a coffee appreciation SIG, and the treasurer of ADCF, a group of Christian students who organize events for people of all backgrounds. Freshman Jules Bello, current leader for the Music Society, echoes this sentiment. “Open Mic was one of those things where we were operating with the expectation that we’d get funds,” Bello said. “The cuts haven’t meant too much yet.” On the other hand, two students commenting on their financial condition only on the basis of anonymity, are attempting to start a new athletic SIG and running into some difficulties. Athletics SIGS are funded mainly by the Athletics Department, which dedicates 12 percent of its budget for SIG funding. “Everyone’s been very helpful,” said one student. “But when it comes down to it, we need money, and the money’s not there.” “The old SIGs get priority funding,” the student’s co-leader added. “The problem with new SIGs is we can’t be certain of how much interest there’ll be. So the Athletics Department might as well put the money where people like it.” After two years of greater flexibility, the Athletics Department – similar to Student Government – is tightening its policies. There is an attendance minimum of 10 people per athletic SIG. “We have to make sure a SIG is valid, that there are 15 to 20 members and not just a couple of friends getting together,” said Wayne Young, Associate Director of Athletics. “SIGs have to hold a certain amount of meetings where attendance is taken.” Student Government is also revising its policies regarding SIGs. As of now, maximum spending limits have been set for food at meetings, and members of the Funding Board will occasionally drop in on meetings to make sure that there is sufficient membership as well. Treasurer Angelina Micha-Djaja said that Student Government has an allotted semester budget from Campus Life, which has remained unchanged this semester. The team is trying to make it clear that the main reason for these cutbacks is not a decrease in finances, but rather a surge of new SIGs this semester. In the past two weeks alone, six new SIGs have been created. “Members of the previous Student Funding Board say it took them a lot less time to go through the budgets for last semester,” Micha-Djaja said. “They had enough money because there were less SIGs who asked for less. Now the mentality’s more like, ‘Oh I got this much last year so let’s try to do more and get more this semester.’ As SIGs try to grow, they are trying to take on more initiatives.” As the university anticipates the arrival of a new freshman class in the fall of 2013, and consequently a slew of more SIGs, it is important, Micha-Djaja said, to consider what is absolutely necessary for funding. Right now, 51 percent of SIG money goes to food – the plethora of pizza, sushi and baked goods that lure in new members and bolster meeting attendance. The spending for this food eats up spending for important SIG resources such as handbells or, for example, art supplies. So while SIGs may be seeing cuts in their pizza funds, this is ultimately because Student Government is trying to help SIGs get the resources they need to fulfill and stay true to their initial missions. “Our goal is to try to work with these SIGs,” Micha-Djaja said. “They contribute to the university’s goals and enrich our education.” Renee Dugan, Assistant Dean of Campus Life, said that both Student Government and Campus Life are working hard to ensure that transparency is a priority for the future. “As we grow, I am sure we will continue to refine our processes to best to ensure that equitable opportunities are available to all groups,” Dugan said. “Minutes from General Assembly meetings are posted after every meeting, and campus life staff meets frequently with Student Government to ensure that policies are developed and rolled out in a thoughtful and effective manner.” Correction: Due to recent changes in university policy we are unable to provide exact expenditure figures. Correction: On March 11, The Gazelle incorrectly reported information regarding expenditures obtained through a miscommunication between the transitory Student Governments. Student Government has updated their final records. The SIGs with the top expenditures were, in fact, the Debate Society and Astronomy Club. The Gazelle regrets this error. Zoe Hu is deputy news editor. Email her at thegazelle.org@gmail.com.

posts.title: Room of Requirement founder hopes legacy will live on at Saadiyat
posts.markdown: Photo credit: via facebook.com It is hard to believe NYUAD went through an entire year before Room of Requirement was created. The Facebook group is essential for students posting information about events and obtaining — or in some cases, retaining — cooking supplies, food and books of all sorts. The social media hub is synonymous with campus life at NYUAD. Given its familiar name and vast use among the student population, it is remarkable that the concept was created by just one individual, junior Mark Hoffman. “It was the summer in between our freshman year and before sophomore year,” Hoffman explained. “Before any of the second year students arrived.” At that point, the NYUAD Student Life page was only Facebook resource for the community to share campus news and notifications. This resulted in a confusing clutter of posts from lost student IDs to where students could find free food. “Originally, people wanted a lost and found page,” Hoffman said. “But, I figured it would be better if it was a ‘whatever you require,’ so that it wasn’t so specific as a lost and found page. No one is really going to check a lost and found page if they haven’t lost anything.” After adding a few students to RoR, Hoffman described its growth as a chain effect, and that “within a couple of hours it was pretty much the whole school.” Granted, the inaugural class was only 150 students so it did not take long for everyone to catch word of the latest addition to the community. The group’s name is a reference to “Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix.” In the book, the room only appears when a character desperately needs it. While it may have been the inspiration for the page, RoR has expanded far beyond an as-needed basis. It has become a staple to the school’s culture, reflecting the tight-knit and helpful manner of the community. Sophomore Valentina Vela described it as the perfect example of community at NYUAD. “I have been able to find information regarding Abu Dhabi, NYU, and more immediate things like where to buy ginger at 2am or how late the buses run,” Vela said. “Room of Requirement connects us, and it allows us to be actively thinking about the needs of others while also feeling cared for." NYUNY Junior Jessica de Oliveira remembers the first time she posted on RoR as a study abroad student this fall. “It took me a while to feel comfortable enough posting in it,” de Oliveira said. “The trajectory of my comfort levels here is definitely related to how comfortable I felt posting in Room of Requirement. I remember the first time I posted. I looked at my post — I read it over a few times and edited it. I wanted to give everyone the right impression with my first.” Despite studying in Berlin this semester, Hoffman admits that he still checks RoR to get a taste of what is happening in Sama Tower while away. “I don’t know many of the freshmen,” Hoffman explains. “It’s also a nice way to gauge with how the community is changing as well.” As the move to Saadiyat approaches, Hoffman believes it will be up to the freshmen class to establish the transition for a sustainable RoR. “The thing with Room of Requirement is I didn’t really ask people, ‘do you want this?’” Hoffman said. “Eventually freshmen will stop asking, ‘Can we make another page?’ and they will just make another page because they’re annoyed.” While he created the inaugural version of RoR, Hoffman is not participating in the transition for the page due to obligations he anticipates for next year such as his capstone project. “Eventually there will be a need for a more efficient way to allocate information,” Hoffman said. Overall, the creator of RoR does hope to see the name continue. “I think it would be fun if 20 years from now, Room of Requirement is maybe some futuristic type of page or maybe a real place on campus,” he said. Nina Bayatti is managing editor. Email her at thegazelle.org@gmail.com.
